title: Role of Local Structural Variation in X-ray Photoelectron Spectrum of Silicon Oxide Interfaces
authors: Mikael Santonen, Sari Granroth, Johanna Laaksonen, Pekka Laukkanen, Johannes Niskanen
abstract: We show that the broad X-ray photoelectron lines of silicon oxide on silicon arise from a continuous statistical distribution of core-level binding energies. Statistical simulations spanning compositions from Si to SiO$_2$ reproduce the full extent of this broadening, reaching 5 eV for SiO$_{1.0}$ , in quantitative agreement with 0.23 nm layer-resolved spectra reconstructed from Ar$^+$ sputtering data. This continuous distribution blurs distinct spectral fingerprints of local structural motifs, thereby challenging conventional chemical state assignment in oxide X-ray photoelectron spectra.
summary: This work investigates how structural randomness in silicon oxide interfaces broadens X-ray photoelectron spectra. By combining MD simulations with DFT calculations, the authors show that spectral broadening results not from multiple distinct chemical states, but from a continuous statistical distribution of binding energies dictated by local atomic arrangements.
main_problem: The study challenges conventional chemical state assignments in oxide X-ray photoelectron spectra by demonstrating that core-level binding energies arise from a continuous distribution governed by local structural variation.
main_result: Statistical simulations successfully reproduce the observed spectral broadening, showing that intermediate stoichiometry regions exhibit wide energy spreads rather than distinct, discrete spectral fingerprints.
method: The research combines Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations with Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations to generate ensemble averages of core-level binding energies from amorphous silicon oxide structures.
model_or_system: The system under investigation is the $	ext{SiOx}$ interface, modeled using supercells derived from MD quench simulations spanning varying oxygen concentrations ($x$). The analysis focuses on how local structural disorder influences electronic properties.
key_observables: Core-level binding energies ($	ext{O } 1s$ and $	ext{Si } 2s$), spectral broadening (up to $5 	ext{ eV}$), depth profiles reconstructed from sputtering, and structural descriptors like the void distribution curve.
important_parameters: The analysis is sensitive to local structure variations over a radius of approximately $5 	ext{ Å}$, and simulations cover compositions from pure Si to $	ext{SiO}_2$.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include treating the observed spectrum as an integral over underlying layers (sputtering model) and assuming constant ionization cross-sections for DFT calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate conceptual XPS build-up, layer-resolved spectra comparisons with simulations, correlation plots between BE shifts and structural descriptors ($D(R)$), and void size distributions for $	ext{SiO}_2$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the experimental challenge (XPS interpretation in disordered oxides), developing simulation tools (DFT/MD), quantifying the structural disorder using descriptors, and finally demonstrating that this continuous variation explains the observed spectral broadening.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state spectroscopy, the methodology of linking macroscopic spectroscopic features to underlying statistical distributions arising from quenched disorder is highly relevant to understanding complex many-body systems where local environments dictate global properties.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The build-up of an X-ray photoelectron spectrum in surface-oxidized silicon. The chemical shift for an atom depends on the local oxygen number density ρO(r), which decays towards bulk silicon. In case of oxygen, the native sig- nal strength at depth r is inherently proportional to ρO(r), whereas for silicon the respective number density ρSi(r) and native signal strength vary less. Attenuation due to inelastic electron scattering yields an exponentially decaying factor for the native signal in the depth-integrated spectrum. The free mean path λph of the incident photon is assumed to be or- ders of magnitude longer than the free mean path λel of the photoelectron.
